chapter: Bix, success and the American Dream
title: Bix's life, approval-seeking, and being victimized by changing values
summary: Rose says Bix sought approval and applause, but he judges musicians by music alone. John cites Frank Power linking Bix and Charlie Parker as victims of changing values, and asks about the Depression.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: But, in a sense, he, couldn't one say he didn't even care? That he just wanted to play his horn?

Well, you wouldn't be able to hear that in his horn. And you would have to know something about his life then. However, it seemed to me that he was constantly, he spent most of his life in search of approval. And he looked for the applause and he gloried in the response. He was not a congenital hermit by any means. And so, however, I am really never inclined to estimate a musician by his life, but only by his music. And what I hear is all I know.

Now, it's been said that, and I think Frank Power said this in a tape that he did in Bidebeck's life, that there was only one other musician that bare any resemblance to Bix Bidebeck. In the sense that both these musicians were victimized by the changing values of their time. And he mentions Charlie Parker. Now, I don't want to talk about, I don't want to bring up Charlie Parker. I'd rather talk about Bix Bidebeck. But, it's very interesting to me that he should bring up Charlie Parker in the relationship to Bix Bidebeck. Because I had decided before, even he had mentioned this, that these two figures, to me, were the ones that I was going to deal with. Because both of them resembled, in some way or another, something very close together. And I'm trying to figure out what it is. But I'm very interested in Frank Power's idea that Bidebeck was victimized by the changing social values of his time. And you're mentioning the shifting nature of the success myth and the elusive quality of the American dream. Did the depression, in a sense, would that be a good marking point for the failure of the American dream, in a sense that everything was confused now?
